Posted on[October 13, 2026](https://www.quicklogic.com/2026/10/13/when-a-bitstream-is-a-liability-the-case-for-antifuse-fpgas/)


by[Mao Wang](https://www.quicklogic.com/author/maowang/)


Reconfigurability is usually treated as an FPGA’s defining advantage. But in some systems, it is also a source of risk.


Many SRAM-based FPGAs power up unconfigured. Before they can operate, configuration data must be retrieved from external or on-chip nonvolatile storage, transferred into configuration SRAM, and protected throughout that process. That architecture is flexible, but it introduces dependencies that affect startup time, standby power, security analysis, and system qualification.


For an instant-on controller, a remote battery-powered sensor, or safety-related aerospace and defense electronics, those dependencies may be unacceptable. In those applications, permanence can be more valuable than reconfigurability.


That is where antifuse FPGAs earn their place.


## **The configuration is a physical connection**


QuickLogic antifuse FPGAs use ViaLink® technology. Each programmable point begins as a high-impedance via between two metal layers. During programming, an applied voltage creates a permanent, low-resistance conductive path across the via—the inverse of opening a conventional fuse, and the origin of the term *antifuse* .


The result is fundamentally different from a charge-based configuration cell. The FPGA routing configuration is embodied in permanent programmed interconnects. It does not need to be loaded from an external bitstream at power-up, and there is no conventional rewritable configuration memory containing the routing configuration.


Devices are programmed once, either through QuickLogic’s programming service or with supported programming equipment before installation. They are not reconfigured in-system after deployment.


That architectural choice delivers three practical advantages.


### **Deterministic, instant-on operation**


Because the FPGA configuration is already present when power is applied, there is no configuration-bitstream loading stage to complete before the programmed logic becomes available. This removes one source of startup delay and failure from the FPGA configuration path.


The complete system must still satisfy its specified power-ramp, reset, clock, and peripheral-startup requirements. But for time-critical control, communications, and munitions applications, removing configuration loading can make startup behavior quicker, simpler, and more deterministic.


### **A smaller configuration attack surface**


A loadable FPGA configuration may exist in storage and travel across a board-level interface during startup. The entire path from source to destination may require protection.


With antifuse technology, there is no external configuration bitstream in transit and no conventional configuration memory from which to read the routing data. That does not make a system immune to every invasive or physical attack, but it substantially reduces the attack surface associated with a stored and loadable FPGA configuration dataset.


### **Very low standby power**


Antifuse configuration requires no configuration-memory refresh or power-up reload. QuickLogic characterizes its ViaLink architecture as providing very low standby power, making it attractive where battery life and thermal margin are constrained. Actual device and system power still depends on the selected part, operating conditions, clock activity, I/O loading, and implemented design.


## **When permanence becomes a safety consideration**


The value of fixed configuration is especially clear in fuze and safe-and-arm (S&A) electronics.


**MIL-STD-1316F** states that safety-related logic in a fuzing system must not be erasable, alterable, or reconfigurable by credible environments that the system would otherwise survive. It also directs implementations using logic devices to be evaluated in accordance with **JOTP-051** , the *Technical Manual for the Use of Logic Devices in Safety Features* .


QuickLogic’s one-time-programmable antifuse fabric implements the FPGA configuration as permanent physical interconnects rather than rewritable, charge-based configuration memory. This makes the technology well suited to fixed-in-structure safety implementations.


That is not an automatic compliance claim. The applicable Service Safety Authority determines whether a specific implementation is acceptable after evaluating the complete design, its safety architecture, verification evidence, and operating environments.


The distinction matters because JOTP-051 adds integrity-validation requirements when charge-based memory implements a safety feature. Those requirements include validating memory integrity before execution of the safety function, with CRC-based verification applying where specified. Because an antifuse FPGA’s routing configuration is not stored in charge-based configuration memory, those configuration-memory validation requirements do not apply to the antifuse configuration itself.


Other required diagnostics, analyses, verification activities, and approvals still apply. Antifuse changes part of what must be demonstrated; it does not remove the obligation to demonstrate safety.


## **Choosing the right antifuse family**


QuickLogic offers a range of antifuse FPGA families, from compact devices with fewer than 1,000 logic cells to larger devices with embedded memory, clock-management, and computational resources.


Explore the[QuickLogic Antifuse FPGA product page](https://www.quicklogic.com/fpgas/antifuse-review/) to compare device families, review specifications, and access datasheets. Because availability and new-design recommendations vary by device and package, contact QuickLogic to confirm the best option for your application.


## **The engineering trade**


Antifuse does not replace SRAM-based FPGAs everywhere. It makes a deliberate trade: field reconfigurability is exchanged for permanent configuration, instant-on behavior, very low standby power, and a smaller configuration-related attack surface.


If a system must start predictably, protect its FPGA configuration without managing a loadable bitstream, or support a safety case in which unintended reconfiguration is a central concern, that trade deserves serious consideration.


*Sometimes the best bitstream is the one the deployed system never needs.*
